title: The Great Stink that cleaned London
text: {{1}} the summer of 1858 the Thames stank so foully {{2}} Members of Parliament fled the riverside chamber with handkerchiefs pressed over their faces. The river had become an open sewer, reeking {{3}} untreated waste, and cholera epidemics had already killed tens of thousands. Parliament {{4}} finally shamed into action, and Joseph Bazalgette, {{5}} ambitious sewer schemes had been shelved for years, was suddenly given the funds to build them. The main sewers were completed {{6}} six years, the embankments that grace the river today were raised to carry the great pipes, and the system put an end {{7}} the worst cholera outbreaks. Bazalgette's tunnels still serve London, {{8}} is a fine reminder that infrastructure, built well, can outlive everyone who argues about it.

gaps.explanation: Seasons take 'in': in the summer of 1858.
'So … that' — degree followed by the result clause.
Past passive with a singular collective subject: was shamed.

gaps.hint: relative: Bazalgette, ___ schemes had been shelved
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' links the engineer to his schemes.
'Within six years' — completed inside that period.

gaps.hint: preposition: put an end ___ the outbreaks
gaps.explanation: 'Put an end to' is the fixed phrase.
Sentential relative after the comma; 'that' is impossible here.
